The tiled corridor curves through warmer air scented with eucalyptus and mineral water. Frosted glass doors open into changing rooms and small treatment rooms, but the corridor itself continues toward a high pool hall overlooking the sea.

The main pool is long and rectangular, its far edge aligned perfectly with the horizon through a wall of glass. Pale blue tile darkens toward the deep end. Steam hangs lightly over the surface even though the room is warm.

Ahead, glass doors lead to an outdoor infinity pool cut into the cliffside below the terrace. To the left, a quiet room contains heated stone loungers beneath a ceiling painted with drifting clouds. To the right, a narrow stair descends toward older baths carved directly into the cliff rock.

Near the indoor pool, a brass rack holds folded white towels embroidered with different room numbers. One towel bears no number at all, only a small stitched outline of the offshore island.
places.name: departures:d10r

places.description:
The dining room and bar occupy a suite of connected rooms behind the lobby, darker and more intimate than the sea-facing spaces. White cloths are laid on round tables beneath shaded brass lamps. Tall windows look into an interior courtyard planted with citrus trees and climbing jasmine.

The bar itself is long, polished, and almost black, backed by mirrored shelves of bottles whose labels are recognizable only by color and shape. A bowl of green olives sits beside a cutting board with one lemon half-wrapped in linen. Low instrumental music plays from a radio cabinet with no visible station dial.

Ahead, glass doors open into the courtyard where small tables sit beneath the trees. To the left, a narrow supper room glows red beneath fabric lampshades. To the right, a staircase descends toward a wine cellar and something that smells strongly of bread baking.

At one table, four place settings surround a centerpiece of white flowers. Three glasses contain water. The fourth contains a folded paper crane.
places.name: departures:d10b

places.description:
A light wooden door faced with layers of painted paper beneath a clear protective coating. The design is faded and crowded: lantern shapes, dark water, narrow roofs, gold lines, red brushstrokes, tiny figures whose faces have been worn away by time. A simple black handle has been wrapped in braided cord.

The door is almost weightless when touched. Warm air occasionally leaks around its edges carrying the smells of grilled spices, citrus smoke, river water, incense, and sugar.

Very faintly, there is noise on the other side—not one sound but many: conversation, laughter, bowls touching, a stringed instrument, and someone calling something unintelligible from a distance.
places.name: the painted paper door

places.description:
Night presses close around a river district bright with lanterns. Narrow buildings lean over stone streets and wooden balconies. Red, gold, green, and blue lights hang in rows beneath eaves and across alleys, reflected everywhere in rain-dark paving and the black surface of the river nearby.

Unlike the other destinations, this place is plainly alive. People move through the streets in loose evening crowds: couples sharing skewers from paper trays, children chasing one another beneath lantern strings, vendors leaning over steaming pots, musicians tuning instruments under awnings. Their clothing varies too widely to belong to a single period or place, yet nobody seems surprised by anyone else.

Ahead, the main market street runs between food stalls and tiny shops toward a brightly lit square crowded around a low stage. To the left, stone steps descend to the river where narrow boats wait beneath lanterns. To the right, a stair climbs between buildings toward rooftop terraces threaded with lights and music. Behind, a quieter lane slips away from the market toward tea rooms, courtyards, and a row of little workshops still open late.

No one stops to explain where you are. A passing vendor offers a paper cone of something hot and fragrant, waits exactly long enough for a decision, then grins and moves on.

Somewhere nearby, a bell rings three times and the whole street cheers for reasons that remain completely unclear.
places.name: departures:d11

places.description:
The main market street grows brighter and noisier toward the square. Steam rolls from copper pots. Flatbreads blister on hot stones. Skewers of vegetables, fish, and unfamiliar fruit hiss over charcoal. A woman behind one stall slices something citrus-bright into a bowl and throws in a handful of herbs without measuring anything.

The square ahead is packed loosely around a low wooden stage hung with paper lanterns. A six-piece band is playing something fast enough to pull people into a rough circle dance, though half the dancers appear to be inventing the steps as they go. Nobody objects.

Ahead, the crowd parts around the stage toward another street lined with fabric canopies. To the left, a narrow arcade contains dessert stalls and little tables. To the right, a game lane glitters with wheels, dice, carved tokens, and prizes nobody seems to take very seriously.

Near the edge of the square, a chalkboard carries tonight's program. Every event is legible except the next one, which has been enthusiastically crossed out and replaced with: WE'LL SEE.
places.name: departures:d11f

places.description:
Stone steps descend from the market street to a river quay slick with reflected lantern light. Narrow wooden boats are tied two and three deep along the edge, some with curved roofs, some open to the night. Boatkeepers sit on low stools drinking tea, talking among themselves, and calling out prices or destinations in a language that somehow remains comprehensible at the level of intention rather than words.

The river is broad and slow. Lanterns float downstream in loose clusters, each carrying a tiny candle protected beneath paper. Buildings along both banks rise in layered balconies and rooflines, their lights broken by dark alleys and small gardens.

Ahead, one boat is preparing to leave for the opposite bank, where a temple-like roof and a line of blue lanterns are visible. To the left, the quay follows the river toward a bridge crowded with pedestrians and musicians. To the right, a quieter landing serves small boats heading downstream beneath trees hung with white lights.

One old boatkeeper points toward the water, then toward the sky, and laughs as if the joke should be obvious. Looking down, the reflected moon is full. Looking up, there is no moon at all.
places.name: departures:d11l

places.description:
The stair climbs steeply between two narrow buildings, passing open kitchen windows and balconies strung with drying herbs. At the top, the roofs flatten into terraces connected by short bridges, ladders, and stairways that make the upper district feel like another city laid over the first.

Tables occupy many of the terraces. Some are crowded with friends sharing bottles and small plates. Others hold only plants, lanterns, or laundry. Music travels unpredictably across the rooftops: a flute from somewhere below, hand drums from across the river, singing from a terrace hidden behind climbing vines.

Ahead, a bridge leads to a larger rooftop garden beneath dozens of hanging lanterns. To the left, narrow steps climb toward a tiny observatory dome painted dark blue. To the right, a line of terraces continues above the river toward a roof where people are releasing small paper lanterns into the air.

From up here, the district's streets form no obvious grid. Several alleys visible below appear to end beneath buildings that, from this height, clearly have courtyards beyond them.
places.name: departures:d11r

places.description:
The quieter lane behind the market is narrow enough that awnings nearly meet overhead. The noise of the main street softens into individual sounds: a teapot lid clicking, a saw rasping through wood, a brush tapping against a ceramic rim, someone laughing behind a paper screen.

Small workshops remain open late. One displays hand-bound notebooks and boxes of loose paper. Another is crowded with carved wooden toys and mechanical birds. A third contains shelves of tiny glass bottles filled with colored powders, dried leaves, metallic flakes, and things that might be spices or pigments.

Ahead, the lane bends toward a courtyard occupied by tea tables beneath a single broad tree. To the left, a workshop door stands open onto a room where paper lanterns are being painted by hand. To the right, a narrow passage leads toward the sound of a fountain and the warm glow of a bathhouse sign.

At a bookbinder's stall, a basket marked FREE contains scraps too small for full pages. One bears a fragment of printed text in plain language: IF YOU FOUND THIS STREET BY ACCIDENT, YOU DID IT CORRECTLY.
places.name: departures:d11b

places.description:
A broad door of smoked glass stands among the mismatched doors of the departure lounge, nearly black until someone comes close. A hair-thin seam of soft violet light runs around the inside of its frame. The light does not blink or pulse; it simply seems to notice proximity.

The glass remains opaque from this side, though now and then a muted wash of color or indistinct movement passes somewhere beyond it and is gone before it can be identified. A narrow handle of dark metal sits flush against the surface. It is smooth, slightly warm, and entirely free of ornament.

At the threshold, the air carries faint smells of rain on warm pavement, bruised green leaves, the dry mineral scent of heated ceramic, and electrical ozone. Under them is the unmistakable smell of something savory cooking somewhere beyond. A low, nearly subliminal mechanical hum comes through the frame, as if from distant machinery or transit.

Nothing on the door names a destination.
places.name: the smoked-glass door

places.description:
Evening opens across a broad elevated concourse woven between tall buildings and open sky. The architecture is advanced without being pristine: stone-composite paving worn smooth at the centers of paths, glass balustrades carrying scratches and fingerprints, old metal handrails polished by use, climbing plants spilling from terraces above. Thin bands of light are set into the pavement and undersides of bridges rather than hung as advertisements, and quiet transit lines slide through lower levels with a soft magnetic hum.

The district is crowded, but comfortably so. Humans move among synthetic residents of many forms: humanoid bodies in ordinary clothes, compact wheeled frames carrying parcels, articulated maintenance walkers, small hovering couriers, tall narrow machines whose faces are arrangements of light rather than features. Nobody treats any of this as remarkable. A human child leans against the leg of a broad-shouldered synthetic guardian while watching trains below. Two mechanical residents argue amiably beside a noodle stall. At a repair kiosk, a woman holds a replacement panel steady while a four-legged field unit clicks it into its own shoulder housing.

There are smells of toasted grain, broth, hot ceramic, wet leaves, machine coolant, tea, ozone after rain, and something sweet being caramelized nearby. Music drifts from somewhere ahead, interrupted occasionally by the soft tones of arriving transit.

Ahead, the concourse broadens toward a lively public promenade of food counters, shops, tables, and music. To the left, workshop lights glow beneath signs for repair, fabrication, fitting, and materials. To the right, open skywalks climb toward terraces overlooking the transit lanes and the city beyond. Behind, a quieter civic interior opens through wide glass bays into reading rooms, rest spaces, galleries, and shared public halls.

Nobody welcomes you to the future. Everyone appears to be busy living in it.
places.name: departures:d12

places.description:
The concourse opens into a broad public promenade beneath a high canopy of glass and suspended greenery. Tables spill from food counters into the walking space without quite blocking it. Steam rises from bowls and kettles. A baker slides flat rounds from a ceramic oven while, two stalls over, a synthetic vendor with four delicate hands assembles intricate layered snacks faster than anyone seems able to eat them.

Humans and machine-bodied residents share long communal tables. Some eat; some connect slim charging leads beneath the benches; some do both sorts of lingering in company. A pair of small courier drones has abandoned all apparent urgency to watch a street musician coax harmonics from a bowed metal instrument. Nobody tells them to move along.

Ahead, the promenade reaches a circular plaza where several overlapping performances are competing amicably for an audience. To the left, an arcade of food counters and tiny tea rooms curves beneath hanging gardens. To the right, public tables continue toward shops selling clothing, modular body fittings, books, toys, tools, scent cartridges, ceramics, and things whose purpose is not immediately obvious.

At one table, three friends are arguing over whether a song was better before or after somebody translated it into a format one of them could actually hear. Their disagreement sounds ancient.
places.name: departures:d12f

places.description:
The left-hand district narrows into a chain of open workshops and repair bays, their fronts rolled back to the evening air. Nothing here resembles a hospital, showroom, or factory. It feels closer to a neighborhood of tailors, bicycle shops, instrument makers, and mechanics, except the bodies and objects under repair are far more varied.

A human technician sits cross-legged on a bench while a synthetic resident beside her has one forearm opened into a neat fan of components. They are discussing paint colors, not diagnostics. Farther along, a squat maintenance machine waits patiently while someone fits a new wheel assembly. Across the lane, a young man tests the balance of an artificial hand by passing a ceramic cup back and forth with its owner.

Shelves hold old housings polished smooth by years of use, replacement joints, sensor covers, woven conductive fabrics, small motors, lengths of cable, hand tools, adhesives, and drawers labeled in several visual and tactile systems. New parts sit beside repaired ones without hierarchy.

Ahead, the lane continues toward a repair café where drinks and tools share the same counters. To the left, a materials library displays hundreds of sample plates, fabrics, polymers, woods, ceramics, and responsive surfaces for anyone choosing how something should feel rather than merely function. To the right, a fabrication hall glows behind wide windows as machines quietly build parts one layer at a time.

A small handwritten sign above one bench reads: OLD DOES NOT MEAN OBSOLETE. The word OLD has been crossed out and replaced with FAMILIAR.
places.name: departures:d12l

places.description:
The right-hand route climbs by shallow ramps and open stairs toward a chain of skywalks suspended between towers. Evening wind moves through the railings carrying the smell of rain, tea, warm metal, and flowering vines from gardens built into the upper levels.

From here the city unfolds in depth: transit lines crossing at several heights, silent lifts moving inside glass shafts, pedestrian bridges threading between illuminated terraces, rooftop farms and darkened maintenance decks, aircraft or drones moving in orderly streams farther out. Nothing dominates the skyline. It is less a collection of monuments than a vast accumulation of useful places.

People linger along the overlooks. A humanoid synthetic resident sits with a cup balanced between both hands though there is no obvious reason it needs warmth. Nearby, two humans and a many-legged machine have arranged themselves around the same low table facing the view. Nobody is speaking.

Ahead, a long terrace follows the transit lanes toward a signal bar where route patterns are projected softly across the tables like weather maps. To the left, a suspended garden incorporates public charging points into deep benches beneath flowering trees. To the right, a narrower bridge leads toward a darker observation deck closer to the moving lines below.

Every few minutes the nearest transit stream changes routing, and a gentle wave of colored light moves through the district as thousands of paths reorganize. Several regulars look up to watch it happen.
places.name: departures:d12r

places.description:
Behind the arrival concourse, the noise softens beneath a wide civic gallery built around several interior courtyards. Glass walls, pale stone, dark wood, woven acoustic panels, and living plants make the space feel warm rather than institutional. There are no checkpoints and no obvious reception desk.

Long reading tables hold printed books, flexible screens, tactile maps, projection surfaces, and interfaces whose purposes become clear only when someone uses them. In one alcove a human reader turns pages beside a synthetic resident receiving the same text as shifting lines of light across its forearms. Farther on, a charging lounge shares space with ordinary chairs, couches, floor cushions, and a low fountain. Some residents are connected to power. Others are asleep. Nobody appears to regard these as fundamentally different activities.

A gallery along one wall holds small objects with brief labels: repaired components, letters, obsolete connectors, children's drawings, fragments of architecture, photographs, machine-cast memories rendered as color and sound. The collection seems less concerned with technological milestones than with things somebody cared enough to keep.

Ahead, the commons continues toward a public memory gallery where visitors can leave short impressions rather than formal records. To the left, a reading room descends around an indoor garden. To the right, a quiet rest hall opens toward a terrace under trees. Above, broad stairs lead to an upper chamber where slow suspended forms turn in currents of warm air and changing light.

Near the entrance, a small plaque reads: REST IS NOT A FAILURE STATE.
places.name: departures:d12b

places.description:
A narrow wooden boat slips away from the quay with barely a sound beyond the knock of water against its hull. Lanterns from the market stretch into long broken ribbons behind you. Midstream, the city seems to separate into layers: warm gold and red on the bank you left, cooler blue light gathering ahead, and between them a broad dark surface carrying the impossible reflection of a full moon.

The boatkeeper does not row in the ordinary sense. A long steering oar rests beneath one hand while the current appears to do most of the work. Halfway across, several floating lanterns drift past in the opposite direction. One goes dark as it passes beneath the boat and relights a few seconds later downstream.

The opposite landing rises in shallow stone steps beneath a line of blue lanterns. Above them stands a low temple-like roof attached to a cluster of courtyards, tea rooms, and covered walkways rather than a single monumental building. People come and go carrying cups, wrapped parcels, small instruments, and baskets of flowers. Two synthetic-looking mechanical birds—whether toys, pets, or something else is unclear—hop along the railing pecking at droplets of wax.

Ahead, the steps climb beneath the blue lanterns into the courtyard district. To the left, a covered walk follows the river under carved eaves toward a quieter garden. To the right, another landing serves small late boats heading farther along the opposite bank.

As the boat touches stone, the old boatkeeper taps the gunwale twice, points at the moon in the water, and then points at the empty sky again. This time he does not laugh.
places.name: departures:d11lf

places.description:
The quay runs left beneath strings of lanterns toward a broad stone bridge crowded with pedestrians, musicians, vendors, and people who seem to have come here mostly to lean on the parapet and watch the river.

The closer you get, the more the music separates into parts: hand drums on the near side, a bowed string instrument halfway across, and a loose brass trio near the far arch playing something mournful enough that several passing children have decided to dance to it anyway.

Small stalls have colonized the bridge approaches. One sells hot chestnuts and tea. Another offers folded paper boats with candles tucked into them. A third appears to rent blankets by the hour to anyone intending to stay and watch the water.

Ahead, the bridge arches over the river toward a dense neighborhood of narrow balconies and late-night kitchens. To the left, stairs descend to a lower riverside walk almost level with the water. To the right, a small landing beneath the bridge is crowded with moored skiffs and musicians taking turns between sets.

At the bridge's midpoint, the river's impossible full moon lies directly below. People step around that particular patch of reflected light without discussing why.
places.name: departures:d11ll

places.description:
The quay grows quieter to the right. Market noise thins behind you until the river and the soft creak of mooring ropes become louder than the crowd. Trees lean over the water here, their branches threaded with small white lights that sway independently of the wind.

A narrow landing serves low boats with covered seats and little brass lamps at bow and stern. Their keepers speak softly, naming downstream stops with gestures toward dark stretches of bank, garden walls, and distant clusters of lanterns.

Ahead, the landing continues beneath the trees toward a riverside garden where white lights hang almost to the ground. To the left, a shallow flight of steps climbs to a row of late tea houses with their windows open to the river. To the right, a boat is taking on passengers for somewhere farther downstream, beyond the last visible bridge.

A woman waiting with a basket of flowers tears one blossom into three pieces and drops them into the current one by one. The first two drift downstream. The third moves briefly against the current before joining them.

Nobody watching reacts.
places.name: departures:d11lr

places.description:
The blue-lantern steps rise into a cluster of connected courtyards beneath low tiled roofs. This is not a temple complex so much as a neighborhood that has borrowed temple architecture for ordinary evening life. Tea rooms open directly onto stone paving. Flower sellers work from shallow alcoves. Musicians sit on cushions beneath carved beams while people come and go carrying parcels, cups, and folded umbrellas.

At the largest courtyard, a shallow basin reflects the blue lanterns overhead. People stop at its edge to wash their hands, cool their wrists, or float single petals across the surface. The two mechanical birds from the river rail have followed uphill and are now stalking a dropped sesame seed with absurd seriousness.

A long communal table occupies one side beneath a vine-covered trellis. Several seats remain empty. Nobody appears to be saving them.

The river is visible again through an opening in the roofs, and its moon remains stubbornly present in the water below.
places.name: departures:d11lff

places.description:
The covered walk follows the river beneath carved wooden eaves darkened by age and weather. Blue lanterns hang farther apart here, leaving pools of shadow between them. One side opens to the water through a rhythm of columns; the other is lined with small gardens, stone basins, benches, and paper-screened rooms set back behind narrow verandas.

The crowd thins to pairs and solitary walkers. Someone has left a stack of folded blankets on a bench with a handwritten sign that amounts to TAKE ONE IF YOU ARE COLD. Near the river rail, an elderly couple share a pot of tea without speaking while watching floating lanterns drift below.

A small garden at the end of the walk surrounds a twisted pine growing from pale gravel. Its branches have been trained outward over the river for so long that the tree seems to be leaning deliberately into the reflection of the moon.

Nothing here asks to be solved. It is simply quieter than the market on the other bank.
places.name: departures:d11lfl

places.description:
The right-hand landing is smaller and more practical, built around boats that work the opposite bank after the main market begins to quiet. Brass lamps hang from short posts. A chalk board lists downstream stops in several scripts, though the times beside them have been rubbed away and rewritten often enough to become a grey fog.

Passengers wait on narrow benches with baskets, instruments, wrapped bundles, and sleepy children. One boatkeeper is repairing a split oar with cord and resin while another pours tea from a battered metal flask into three mismatched cups.

Across the water, the market glows red and gold. From this angle its noise arrives softened and out of sequence: first laughter, then music, then the sharp clatter that probably caused the laughter several seconds earlier.

A tiny brass bell hangs beside the mooring post. Nobody rings it. Every arriving boat seems to know when somebody is waiting.
places.name: departures:d11lfr

places.description:
The bridge rises gently over the river, wide enough for two streams of pedestrians and still somehow occupied by people standing still. Vendors have learned to fit themselves into every widening of the parapet. Steam from chestnuts and tea mixes with the cold damp smell of stone.

At the crest, the three groups of musicians can finally hear one another. They are not playing the same piece, but after several minutes their rhythms begin accidentally interlocking. A cluster of dancers has formed in the middle and is taking credit for this development.

The opposite end of the bridge disappears into a neighborhood of narrow balconies and late kitchens whose open windows throw rectangles of warm light onto wet paving. From the highest point, both banks and most of the lantern river are visible at once.

Directly below, the reflected full moon sits in the current like a dropped coin too large for anyone to retrieve. Pedestrians give that patch of light a little extra room without ever looking conspicuously at it.
places.name: departures:d11llf

places.description:
Stone stairs descend from the bridge approach to a narrow riverside walk only a little above the waterline. The underside of the bridge turns the music overhead into a warm, distant thunder of footsteps, bass notes, and occasional applause.

The path is damp and cool. Small lamps are set into the retaining wall at ankle height, illuminating moss, old flood marks, and niches containing cups, flowers, coins, and folded scraps of paper. Nobody nearby appears to be collecting them.

A low stone bench faces the river from beneath the central arch. From here the market lights fracture across the current, and the impossible moon reflection becomes elongated enough to look almost like a road.

A stray dog sleeps under the bench with the calm entitlement of something that has correctly concluded the city belongs to it.
places.name: departures:d11lll

places.description:
Beneath the bridge, a sheltered landing holds half a dozen narrow skiffs tied close together. Musicians use the stone ledge between sets, drinking tea, restringing instruments, and pretending not to listen when another group above starts a song they know.

An old brass brazier gives off enough heat to dry gloves and warm hands. Beside it sits a crate of mismatched cups and a dented kettle maintained communally by whoever notices it first.

The river here is dark except where lantern reflections reach beneath the arch. The moon-reflection does not enter the shadow of the bridge. It stops at the edge of darkness with an unnervingly clean boundary, resumes on the other side, and nobody remarks on that either.

One violinist has written a tiny set list on the back of a ferry receipt. The final item is simply: SOMETHING EVERYONE KNOWS.
places.name: departures:d11llr

places.description:
The riverside garden sits beneath trees hung with hundreds of small white lights, some wrapped around branches and others dangling low enough to sway just above head height. The ground is dark gravel broken by patches of moss, stone seats, and shallow channels carrying river water through beds of reeds.

People come here to be quiet without necessarily being alone. A group of friends has spread a cloth beneath one tree and is sharing fruit from a wooden box. An older man reads by the light hanging over his shoulder. Two children are trying to count how many lights blink at exactly the same moment and disagree loudly about the result.

At the garden's river edge, three stone basins collect water from a narrow spillway. The first reflects the white lights. The second reflects only darkness. The third contains the impossible full moon, perfectly centered, despite being several steps inland from the river itself.

A gardener nearby is trimming herbs and either has not noticed or has decided correctly that it is none of his business.
places.name: departures:d11lrf

places.description:
A shallow stair climbs from the quiet landing to a row of tea houses built shoulder to shoulder along the river wall. Their windows fold completely open at night, so the rooms become warm rectangles of wood, steam, low conversation, and shelves of cups facing the dark water.

No two establishments seem to agree on furniture. One uses floor cushions and low tables. Another has narrow booths. A third has only a long counter facing the river, where patrons sit alone together.

Tea comes in small pots, large pots, chipped mugs, delicate bowls, and one place that appears to serve it in squat metal flasks intended to remain hot for hours. Beside several cups sit tiny dishes of salted fruit, roasted seeds, or sweets wrapped in translucent paper.

A menu board lists eight teas and then, beneath them, THE ONE YOU ALREADY ORDERED, priced exactly the same as the others. Nobody at the counter seems bothered by this.
places.name: departures:d11lrl

places.description:
A low covered boat waits at the end of the landing for passengers heading beyond the last visible bridge. Its interior is lined with worn cushions and narrow shelves for baskets and parcels. Two brass lamps cast more light onto the passengers' hands than onto their faces.

The boat does not leave immediately. It fills slowly with people carrying groceries, flowers, tools, folded cloth, and one very sleepy child who is already using a bundled coat as a pillow. The atmosphere is less excursion than late commute.

From the mooring, downstream city lights become sparse enough that individual windows and garden lanterns stand out against long dark stretches of bank. Farther away, beyond the final bridge, a thin horizontal band of pale light sits just above the water and does not appear to belong to any building.

The boatkeeper notices it, squints once, and continues tying a knot. Whatever it is can wait until another night.
places.name: departures:d11lrr
